This project classifies particle types (electrons, positrons, muons, pions, and protons) from liquid argon time projection chamber detector images using convolutional neural networks. Building on the MicroBooNE Collaboration's approach [1], the model learns visual patterns directly from the data rather than relying on hand-engineered physics rules. Through systematic hyperparameter optimization focused on learning rate scheduling, the final model achieves 89.1% validation accuracy.

**Source code**: [github.com/olivia-jackson-lambert/high-energy-particle-classifier](https://github.com/olivia-jackson-lambert/high-energy-particle-classifier)

# Data Exploration

## Particle Types in the Dataset

This dataset contains five charged particle types commonly observed in liquid argon time projection chambers. Each particle differs in mass and electric charge, which strongly influences its track morphology in the detector.

| Particle  | Symbol | Charge (e) | Mass (MeV/c²) | Typical detector signature |
|----------|--------|------------|---------------|----------------------------|
| Electron | e⁻     | −1         | 0.511         | Light, long, branching tracks |
| Positron | e⁺     | +1         | 0.511         | Similar topology to electrons |
| Muon     | μ⁻     | −1         | 105.7         | Long, straight, penetrating tracks |
| Pion     | π⁺     | +1         | 139.6         | Moderately long, hadronic tracks |
| Proton   | p      | +1         | 938.3         | Short tracks with dense energy deposition |

## Example Particle Tracks Across the Momentum Range

The figure below shows example detector images for each particle type, ordered by increasing initial momentum from left to right. Each row shows one of three detector projections (X–Y, Y–Z, Z–X).

Higher-mass particles produce shorter, denser tracks, while lighter particles travel farther and scatter more. These subtle visual differences are what the CNN learns to distinguish.

![](assets/particle_types.gif){fig-alt="Example particle tracks at different initial momentums by type" width="100%"}

## Truth-Level Feature Distributions

Each detector image comes with kinematic and spatial features that provide physical context for the particle trajectories.

The momentum components $p_x$, $p_y$, and $p_z$ are symmetric around zero since particles are equally likely to move in any direction. Total momentum is defined as $p = \sqrt{p_x^2 + p_y^2 + p_z^2}$.

The production coordinates $(x, y, z)$ are bounded and approximately uniform, reflecting the detector geometry.

![](assets/truth_arrays.gif){fig-alt="Truth arrays by particle type" width="100%"}

# Initial Model
## Architecture

The model uses a convolutional neural network with three conv blocks, each containing two convolutional layers with batch normalization and ReLU activation. After each block, max pooling reduces spatial dimensions while dropout provides regularization. The feature maps start at 16 filters and double with each block (16 → 32 → 64), allowing the network to learn increasingly abstract representations of particle tracks.

Global average pooling compresses the final feature maps into a fixed-length vector, which feeds into a small dense layer before the 5-way softmax classifier. This architecture balances expressiveness with efficiency. It is simple enough to train quickly, but with enough capacity to capture the visual patterns that distinguish particle types.

![](assets/init_cnn_architecture_blocks.png){fig-alt="CNN architecture diagram showing three convolutional blocks" fig-align="center" width=70%}

## Initial Model Performance

### Training Dynamics

The model learns quickly, with training and validation accuracy tracking closely. The final training accuracy is 82.9% and validation accuracy is 82.4%, suggesting minimal overfitting.

### Classification Performance

Electrons, positrons, and protons are classified with high accuracy, while muons and pions show more confusion with other particle types. This may be due to particle tracks with similar energies looking visually alike.

![](assets/init_cnn_confusion_matrix.png){fig-alt="Normalized confusion matrix for particle classifier" fig-align="center" width="75%"}

# Hyperparameter Optimization

### First Round Results

The first hyperparameter sweep tested architectural and optimization choices. Learning rate had the strongest impact on performance, with an increase to 2e-3 raising the validation accuracy to 83.2%.

Wider filters and larger dense layers didn't help, suggesting the baseline architecture was already expressive enough. Removing batch normalization significantly hurt performance, while dropout adjustments had minimal effect.

Most models converged within 4-5 epochs, indicating the architecture is well-suited to the data and that the main gains would come from optimization rather than model capacity.

| Configuration          | Key Change                              | Best Validation Accuracy | Final Validation Loss |
|------------------------|------------------------------------------|--------------------------|-----------------------|
| **Higher learning rate** | Increased learning rate (2e-3) | **0.832** | **0.410** |
| Less dropout            | Reduced dropout regularization            | 0.814 | 0.462 |
| Baseline                | Reference architecture                    | 0.813 | 0.464 |
| Average pooling         | Replaced max pooling with average pooling | 0.806 | 0.458 |
| More dropout            | Increased dropout regularization          | 0.790 | 0.501 |
| Wider filters           | Increased convolutional filters           | 0.782 | 0.481 |
| No batch normalization  | Removed batch normalization               | 0.763 | 0.525 |
| Larger dense head       | Increased dense layer width               | 0.759 | 0.515 |
| Lower learning rate     | Reduced learning rate (3e-4)              | 0.721 | 0.607 |

### Second Round Results

The second round tested learning rates more systematically. The first sweep used adaptive learning-rate scheduling for stability, but this round disabled it to isolate the effect of different initial learning rates.

### Impact of Learning Rate Scheduling

Adding learning rate plateau scheduling dramatically improved performance across all initial learning rates. The best configuration (1.0e-3 with plateau) reached 89.1% validation accuracy—a 5.7 percentage point improvement over the fixed rate.

| Initial learning rate | Best val acc (no LR plateau) | Best val acc (with LR plateau) | Improvement |
|----------------------|------------------------------|--------------------------------|-------------|
| 1.0e−3 | 0.834 | **0.891** | +5.7pp |
| 1.2e−3 | 0.679 | 0.735 | +5.6pp |
| 1.5e−3 | 0.633 | 0.820 | +18.7pp |
| 2.0e−3 | 0.654 | 0.832 | +17.8pp |
| 3.0e−3 | 0.641 | 0.844 | +20.3pp |


# Final Model
## Performance Evaluation
### Training Dynamics

The final model trained for 14 epochs with learning rate plateau scheduling. Training was stable throughout, with the learning rate reducing from 1e-3 to 2e-4 at epoch 9, and again to 4e-5 at epoch 12 as validation loss plateaued. The model achieved peak validation accuracy of 89.1% at epoch 10, with training and validation curves remaining close, indicating good generalization without overfitting.

### Classification Performance

The final model achieves **89.1% validation accuracy** - a 6.7 percentage point improvement over the baseline. The confusion matrix shows much better distinction between muons and pions, which were the most challenging classes initially.

![](assets/final_cnn_confusion_matrix.png){fig-alt="Normalized confusion matrix for particle classifier" fig-align="center" width="75%"}

Example predictions show the model correctly classifying particles across different momentum ranges and track morphologies.

![](assets/cnn_example_predictions.png){fig-alt="Example predictions from the final CNN model showing correctly classified particle tracks" width="100%"}

# Next Steps

**Architecture**: Test modern architectures like ResNets or attention mechanisms to better distinguish similar particle types.

**Evaluation**: Evaluate on a held-out test set and add uncertainty quantification to identify low-confidence predictions.

**Explainability**: Use Grad-CAM to visualize which parts of detector images drive predictions, improving model interpretability.

# References
